question: Two stocks have the same expected return of 15%. Stock A has σ = 25%, Stock B has σ = 15%. Which is the better investment?
before: When two investments have the same expected return, the one with lower risk (σ) is unambiguously better — this is the principle of dominance. Stock B dominates Stock A. Higher risk doesn't help when returns are equal.
after:
Concept: The principle of dominance states that when two investments offer identical expected returns, the one with lower volatility (standard deviation) is always preferable because it achieves the same outcome with less fluctuation around that outcome.

Why this is correct: Stock B delivers the same expected return of 15% as Stock A but with a standard deviation of 15% instead of 25%. Since both stocks promise equal return, an investor should rationally choose the investment that exposes them to less variability. This is not a matter of preference or risk appetite — it is pure mathematical dominance. Stock B is objectively better.

Why the others are wrong: Option A (Stock A, because higher risk means higher potential upside) confuses the general risk-return tradeoff with a situation where returns are already equal. Higher risk is only justified when it compensates with higher expected return; here it does not. Option C (They are equal because they have the same expected return) ignores that expected return is only one dimension of investment quality. Risk matters independently — two investments with identical returns are not equivalent if one is riskier. Option D (Cannot determine without knowing their betas) is incorrect because the comparison between these two stocks is self-contained. Beta measures systematic risk relative to a market index and would only matter if we were comparing them to a broader portfolio or benchmark; the dominance principle applies to the two stocks in isolation.

Intuition: In equity research, when screening comparable companies with similar growth prospects or earnings yields, lower-volatility peers represent better risk-adjusted value. The concept of dominance is foundational to portfolio construction — always eliminate dominated securities before building efficient portfolios.
